reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations
chapter_title: Geotechnical Aspects and Limit State Design

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Chapter 7 presents the geotechnical aspects of driven pile foundation design following the AASHTO (2014) LRFD Bridge Design Specifications. This chapter is the most comprehensive in GEC-12 Volume 1, covering all four LRFD limit states as they apply to driven piles: strength, service, extreme event, and fatigue. The fundamental design equation requires factored resistance Rr = phi * Rn to exceed factored loads. The chapter addresses static analysis methods for axial compression, tension, and lateral resistance; pile group behavior; settlement evaluation; downdrag; drivability; and construction considerations. Eight static analysis methods are presented for single pile axial capacity, each with AASHTO-calibrated resistance factors.
key_points: LRFD design: factored resistance Rr = phi * Rn must exceed factored loads
Four limit states covered: strength, service, extreme event, fatigue
Eight static analysis methods for axial capacity with AASHTO-calibrated resistance factors
Resistance factors are method-specific and condition-specific per AASHTO Table 10.5.5.2.3-1
phi = 0.25 to 0.50 for static analysis methods depending on method and soil type
phi = 0.65 to 0.80 for dynamic methods (wave equation, dynamic testing, load tests)
Pile impedance EA/C is the primary parameter controlling drivability
Soil setup and relaxation must be considered in design and construction

Eq 7-2: Rn = Rs + Rp (nominal resistance = shaft + toe)
Eq 7-3: Rs = SUM(f_si * A_si) (shaft resistance from unit shaft resistance times surface area per layer)
Eq 7-4: Rp = q_p * A_t (toe resistance from unit toe resistance times toe area)
Eq 7-5: Rr = phi_stat * (Rs + Rp) (factored resistance using static analysis resistance factor)

sections.applicability: Framework chapter establishing LRFD methodology for all subsequent driven pile geotechnical design calculations. Resistance factors in Tables 7-1 and 7-2 govern all axial capacity analyses.

subsections.title: Driving Point Resistance
subsections.body: Discusses how piles develop resistance through a combination of shaft resistance along the pile perimeter and toe resistance at the pile tip. The relative contribution of shaft versus toe resistance depends on soil conditions and pile geometry.

subsections.title: Resistance Factors
subsections.body: AASHTO (2014) provides resistance factors calibrated for each static and dynamic method. Static analysis methods range from phi = 0.25 to 0.50. Dynamic methods have higher phi values (0.65-0.80) reflecting greater reliability when verified during construction.

subsections.title: Soil Response to Pile Driving
subsections.body: Pile driving causes significant soil disturbance. In cohesionless soils, the disturbed zone extends 3-5 pile diameters (Figure 7-1). In cohesive soils, the remolded zone is about 1-2 pile diameters (Figure 7-2). These disturbances result in time-dependent resistance changes (setup and relaxation).

subsections.title: Changes in Soil Resistance with Time
subsections.body: Shaft resistance in cohesive soils typically increases after driving (soil setup) as excess pore water pressures dissipate. In some cohesionless soils, relaxation can reduce toe resistance after driving. Both phenomena must be considered.

subsections.title: Static Analysis Methods Overview
subsections.body: Eight static analysis methods are presented: Nordlund (cohesionless), Alpha/Tomlinson (cohesive), P2A/API (mixed), Beta/Effective Stress (all soils), Brown/SPT (cohesionless), Eslami-Fellenius/CPT (all soils), and Nottingham-Schmertmann/CPT (all soils).

subsections.title: Software for Static Analysis
subsections.body: Several software programs automate static analysis calculations including APILE, UniPile, AllPile, and SPT97. APILE implements Nordlund, Alpha, P2A (API), and Schmertmann CPT methods. UniPile implements Beta and Eslami-Fellenius methods.

sections.title: Strength Limit States
sections.body: This major section covers the strength limit state design of driven piles under axial compression, tension, and lateral loading. It presents eight static analysis methods for single pile axial capacity, pile group behavior in compression, axial tension resistance, time-dependent resistance changes (setup and relaxation), lateral resistance, pile length estimation, groundwater effects, scour, and downdrag. Each method includes step-by-step procedures, equations, design charts, and AASHTO-calibrated resistance factors.
key_points: Eight static analysis methods for single pile axial compression capacity
Nordlund method is the primary method for cohesionless soils
Alpha (Tomlinson) method is the primary method for cohesive soils
Group capacity is the lesser of sum of individual pile capacities and block failure capacity
Tension resistance limited to 50% of skin friction for Nordlund method
Setup factors can increase long-term resistance 2-5x or more in some clays
Downdrag loads should be considered as additional load, not reduced resistance
sections.applicability: Core design section for driven pile axial and lateral capacity calculations under strength limit states per AASHTO LRFD.

subsections.title: Nominal Axial Compression Resistance of Single Piles
subsections.body: Presents eight static analysis methods for calculating the nominal axial compression resistance of single driven piles. Each method has specific applicability depending on soil type and available subsurface data. The Nordlund method is recommended for cohesionless soils using SPT data, the Alpha method for cohesive soils, the Beta method as a general effective stress approach, and CPT-based methods when cone penetration data are available.
key_points: Nordlund method: primary method for cohesionless soils using SPT correlations
Alpha (Tomlinson) method: total stress method for cohesive soils using undrained shear strength
P2A (API RP2A) method: offshore-derived method applicable to mixed soil profiles
Beta (Effective Stress) method: general method using effective stress parameters
Brown method: SPT N60-based method for cohesionless soils
Eslami-Fellenius method: CPT-based method for all soil types
Nottingham-Schmertmann method: CPT-based method for all soil types
Rock resistance via uniaxial compressive strength (Section 7.2.1.5)
Static analysis software overview (Section 7.2.1.6)

subsections.title: Nordlund Method (Cohesionless Soils)
subsections.body: The Nordlund (1963, 1979) method is the primary static analysis procedure for calculating the shaft and toe resistance of piles driven into cohesionless soils. It accounts for soil displacement volume, pile taper, pile material friction coefficient, and soil friction angle. The method uses four design charts (Figures 7-4 through 7-8) and provides both shaft and toe resistance components. The pile-soil friction angle delta is determined from the pile volume and soil friction angle. A limiting unit toe resistance prevents unrealistic values at depth. This is the most widely used method for driven piles in sand and gravel.
key_points: Primary method for cohesionless soils per AASHTO; phi = 0.45
Shaft resistance depends on soil friction angle, pile displacement volume, pile taper, and pile-soil friction
Unit toe resistance limited by alpha_t coefficient to prevent unrealistic values at depth
Requires soil friction angle (from SPT N-value correlations in Chapter 5)
Step-by-step procedure with 6 design charts (Figures 7-4 through 7-8)
Applicable to timber, steel, and concrete pile types
Correction factor C_F accounts for difference between delta/phi ratio and assumed Nordlund curve
equations: Eq 7-6: Rs = SUM(K_delta * C_F * p_d * cos(omega) * Delta_d / cos(omega)) (shaft resistance)
Eq 7-7: K_delta from charts based on displaced soil volume V and phi
Eq 7-8: Rp = alpha_t * N'_q * A_t (toe resistance)
Eq 7-9: q_L = alpha_t * N'_q (limiting unit toe resistance)

subsections.title: Alpha Method (Cohesive Soils)
subsections.body: The Alpha method (Tomlinson 1957, 1971) is a total stress approach for calculating shaft and toe resistance of piles in cohesive soils. The adhesion factor alpha relates pile-soil adhesion to the soil undrained shear strength. The Alpha method accounts for pile type, soil layering, and the effect of overlying granular deposits on the adhesion of underlying clays. Adhesion values are obtained from Figures 7-9 through 7-11 based on undrained shear strength and pile embedment ratio. Toe resistance is calculated using Nc = 9 bearing capacity factor.
key_points: Total stress method using undrained shear strength su; phi = 0.35
Adhesion factor alpha depends on su, pile type, and soil layering
Three charts for different soil/pile combinations (Figures 7-9 through 7-11)
Figure 7-9: concrete or timber piles in stiff clay without overlying sand
Figure 7-10: concrete or timber piles in stiff clay with overlying sand
Figure 7-11: steel piles in stiff clay (any overlying condition)
Toe bearing capacity factor Nc = 9 for piles penetrating >= 3B into bearing layer
Unit toe resistance: q_p = 9 * su at the pile toe
equations: Eq 7-10: Rs = SUM(c_a * A_si) (shaft resistance from adhesion times surface area)
Eq 7-11: Rp = 9 * s_u * A_t (toe resistance using Nc = 9)

subsections.title: P2A (API RP2A) Method
subsections.body: The P2A method follows the API Recommended Practice 2A-LRFD (1993) for fixed offshore platforms, adapted for onshore driven pile design. It provides both shaft and toe resistance calculations for cohesionless and cohesive soils. For cohesionless soils, the unit shaft resistance is the product of the lateral earth pressure coefficient K and effective overburden stress times tan(delta), with limiting values from Table 7-5. For cohesive soils, the adhesion factor alpha varies from 1.0 for low su/sigma'v ratios to a minimum of 0.5 for high ratios. Toe resistance uses Nq bearing capacity factors from Table 7-5 for sands and Nc = 9 for clays.
key_points: Derived from offshore platform pile design, adapted for onshore use; phi = 0.25
Cohesionless shaft: f_s = K * sigma'_v * tan(delta) with limiting values
Cohesive shaft: alpha ranges from 0.5 to 1.0 based on su/sigma'_v ratio
Cohesionless toe: q_p = sigma'_v * Nq with limiting values from Table 7-5
Cohesive toe: q_p = 9 * su
Relatively low resistance factor (0.25) due to limited calibration data
equations: Eq 7-12: f_s = K * sigma'_v * tan(delta) (unit shaft resistance, cohesionless)
Eq 7-13: alpha = 0.5 * (su/sigma'_v)^(-0.5) for su/sigma'_v <= 1.0
Eq 7-14: alpha = 0.5 * (su/sigma'_v)^(-0.25) for su/sigma'_v > 1.0
Eq 7-15: f_s = alpha * su (unit shaft resistance, cohesive)
Eq 7-16: q_p = sigma'_v * N_q (unit toe resistance, cohesionless)
Eq 7-17: q_p = 9 * su (unit toe resistance, cohesive)
Eq 7-18: R_n = SUM(f_si * A_si) + q_p * A_t (total nominal resistance)

subsections.title: Effective Stress Methods
subsections.body: Two effective stress approaches are presented: the Beta method and the Brown method. The Beta method (Esrig and Kirby 1979) computes shaft and toe resistance using effective stresses and is applicable to all soil types. The Brown method (2001) uses corrected SPT N60 values to estimate capacity in cohesionless soils. Additionally, two CPT-based methods are presented: Eslami-Fellenius and Nottingham-Schmertmann.

subsections.title: Beta Method (Effective Stress)
subsections.body: The Beta method computes unit shaft resistance as the product of the Beta coefficient and the effective overburden stress. The Beta coefficient is related to the soil friction angle and OCR. For normally consolidated clays, Beta typically ranges from 0.2 to 0.3; for overconsolidated clays, Beta can exceed 1.0. Toe resistance uses Nt bearing capacity factor. The method is applicable to all soil types and is the primary method for mixed profiles.
key_points: General effective stress method applicable to all soil types; phi = 0.25
Unit shaft resistance: f_s = Beta * sigma'_v
Beta = K_s * tan(delta), where K_s is the lateral earth pressure coefficient on pile shaft
Normally consolidated clays: Beta = 0.2-0.3; OC clays: Beta up to 2.0
Toe resistance: q_p = N_t * sigma'_vt (Nt from effective stress bearing capacity theory)
Implemented in UniPile software
equations: Eq 7-19: f_s = Beta * sigma'_v (unit shaft resistance)
Eq 7-20: q_p = N_t * sigma'_vt (unit toe resistance)

subsections.title: Brown Method (SPT N60)
subsections.body: Brown (2001) developed a method that uses corrected SPT N60 values to estimate driven pile capacity in cohesionless soils. Unit shaft resistance is computed directly from N60 with depth-dependent coefficients. The method was calibrated against a load test database.
key_points: SPT N60-based method for cohesionless soils; phi = 0.30
Unit shaft resistance from N60 with depth-dependent coefficients
Calibrated against pile load test database
Separate equations for shaft and toe resistance
equations: Eq 7-21: f_s = a * N60 (unit shaft resistance, with depth limits)
Eq 7-22: q_p = b * N60 (unit toe resistance, with limiting value)
Eq 7-23: Coefficients a and b from Table 7-7

subsections.title: Eslami and Fellenius CPT Method
subsections.body: Eslami and Fellenius (1997) developed a CPT-based method that uses the effective cone tip resistance (q_E = q_c - u_2) to estimate pile capacity. Soil is classified into five types based on the relationship between q_E and sleeve friction f_s. A toe coefficient C_t is applied to the geometric average of q_E in the influence zone around the pile toe.
key_points: CPT-based method using effective cone resistance q_E = q_c - u_2; phi = 0.50
Highest resistance factor (0.50) of all static methods due to CPT reliability
Five soil types classified by q_E vs f_s relationship
Shaft resistance: f_s = C_s * q_E where C_s depends on soil type (Table 7-8)
Toe resistance: q_p = C_t * q_Eg (geometric average in influence zone)
Influence zone: 4B below to 4B above pile toe
equations: Eq 7-24: q_E = q_c - u_2 (effective cone tip resistance)
Eq 7-25: f_s = C_s * q_E (unit shaft resistance)
Eq 7-26: q_Eg = (q_E1 * q_E2 * ... * q_En)^(1/n) (geometric average)
Eq 7-27: q_p = C_t * q_Eg (unit toe resistance)
Eq 7-28: C_t and C_s coefficients from Table 7-8

subsections.title: Nottingham and Schmertmann CPT Method
subsections.body: Nottingham and Schmertmann (1975) developed a CPT-based method using the measured cone tip resistance q_c and sleeve friction f_s to estimate pile capacity. The method uses a friction ratio approach for shaft resistance and an averaging technique for toe resistance in the influence zone around the pile toe. Different reduction factors apply to mechanical and electric cone data.
key_points: CPT-based method using q_c and f_s data; phi = 0.50
Shaft resistance uses friction ratio approach with depth-dependent K factors
Toe resistance from cone tip averaging in influence zone (8B below to 4B above toe)
Minimum path rule for averaging toe resistance to prevent overestimation
Different factors for mechanical vs electric cone penetrometers
Implemented in DRIVEN and APILE software
equations: Eq 7-29: f_s = K * f_sc (unit shaft resistance from cone sleeve friction)
Eq 7-30: K factor from Figure 7-14 based on depth and cone type
Eq 7-31: q_p = (q_c1 + q_c2) / 2 * 1/(2*y) (toe resistance average path)
Eq 7-32: q_c1 = average q_c from toe to 0.7-4B below toe (minimum path rule)
Eq 7-33: q_c2 = average q_c from toe to 8B above toe (upward averaging)

subsections.title: Nominal Axial Resistance from Rock
subsections.body: For piles driven to rock, the nominal toe resistance on rock is typically controlled by the structural capacity of the pile section rather than the rock strength. The geotechnical toe resistance in rock can be estimated from the uniaxial compressive strength. For very hard rock, the pile structural resistance controls.
key_points: Rock toe resistance often controlled by pile structural capacity, not rock strength
q_p = 3 * q_u for highly weathered or soft rock (Eq 7-34)
For competent rock: limited by pile structural resistance
Must verify pile can be driven to rock without damage (drivability check)
equations: Eq 7-34: q_p = 3 * q_u (unit toe resistance on weathered/soft rock)

subsections.title: Software Overview for Static Analysis
subsections.body: Several software programs automate static analysis calculations: APILE implements Nordlund, Alpha, P2A, and Schmertmann methods; UniPile implements Beta and Eslami-Fellenius methods; AllPile covers multiple methods; SPT97 is an SPT-based program.
key_points: APILE: Nordlund, Alpha, P2A (API), Schmertmann CPT methods
UniPile: Beta (effective stress) and Eslami-Fellenius CPT methods
AllPile: multiple methods in a single interface
SPT97: SPT N-value based calculations
All programs require engineering judgment to verify input and output

subsections.title: Pile Groups in Compression
subsections.body: Discusses the behavior and capacity of pile groups under axial compression loads. Group capacity may be controlled by the sum of individual pile capacities (modified by group efficiency) or by block failure of the group acting as a unit. The group efficiency factor accounts for interaction effects when piles are closely spaced. AASHTO (2014) requires evaluation of both individual and block failure modes.
key_points: Group capacity = minimum of (sum of individual capacities, block failure capacity)
AASHTO phi for group = 0.65 (individual) or method-specific phi (block failure)
Group efficiency Eg from Converse-Labarre formula for individual pile check
Block failure mode critical for cohesive soils at close spacing
Block failure shaft resistance from perimeter of group; toe from base area
For cohesionless soils, group efficiency typically >= 1.0 at typical spacings (3B c/c)
Minimum spacing 2.5B or 30 inches per AASHTO; 3B preferred
equations: Eq 7-35: Eg = 1 - arctan(d/s) * [(n-1)*m + (m-1)*n] / (90*m*n) (Converse-Labarre efficiency)
Eq 7-36: R_block = 2*D*(B_g+Z_g)*c_a + B_g*Z_g*c_u*N_c (block failure, cohesive soil)
Eq 7-37: R_block_sand = 2*D*(B_g+Z_g)*K*sigma'_v*tan(delta) + B_g*Z_g*alpha_t*N'_q*sigma'_vt (block failure, cohesionless)

subsections.title: Pile Group Efficiency
subsections.body: Group efficiency factor Eg reduces the sum of individual pile resistances to account for interaction. Converse-Labarre formula (Eq 7-35) is the standard approach.

subsections.title: Block Failure in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: For closely spaced piles in cohesive soils, the group may fail as a block with shaft resistance on the perimeter and base bearing on the group footprint area.

subsections.title: Block Failure in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: Block failure in cohesionless soils uses perimeter shaft resistance and base bearing capacity on the group footprint. This mode is rarely critical for typical spacings.

subsections.title: Axial Tension Resistance of Single Piles and Pile Groups
subsections.body: Axial tension (uplift) resistance consists only of shaft resistance; there is no toe contribution. AASHTO specifies reduced resistance factors for tension compared to compression. For groups in uplift, the resistance is the lesser of the sum of individual pile uplift capacities and the weight of the soil block enclosed by the group.
key_points: Tension resistance = shaft resistance only (no toe component)
AASHTO resistance factors for uplift range from 0.15 to 0.35 for static methods
Nordlund method: uplift shaft resistance limited to 50% of compression shaft resistance (Eq 7-38)
Alpha method: uplift uses same adhesion values but with uplift resistance factor
Beta method: uplift shaft resistance same as compression but with uplift phi factor
Group uplift = minimum of individual pile sum and weight of enclosed soil block
Cohesive soils: group uplift includes perimeter adhesion plus soil block weight (Eq 7-41)
equations: Eq 7-38: R_n_uplift = 0.50 * R_s_Nordlund (Nordlund uplift = 50% of compression shaft)
Eq 7-39: R_n_uplift = R_s_Alpha (Alpha method uplift = full shaft resistance)
Eq 7-40: R_group_uplift = min(SUM(R_ni_uplift), W_block) (group uplift)
Eq 7-41: R_group_uplift_cohesive = 2*D*(B_g+Z_g)*c_a + W_g (group uplift in clay)

subsections.title: Single Pile Uplift
subsections.body: Single pile uplift resistance is the shaft resistance calculated by any of the static methods, with method-specific reduction factors applied.

subsections.title: Group Uplift
subsections.body: Group uplift is checked against both the sum of individual pile uplift resistances and the weight of the soil block enclosed by the pile group perimeter.

subsections.title: Group Uplift in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: In cohesionless soils, the group uplift resistance is typically controlled by the sum of individual pile uplift capacities.

subsections.title: Group Uplift in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: In cohesive soils, the group uplift may be controlled by the block failure mode with perimeter adhesion plus the weight of the soil block (Eq 7-41).

subsections.title: Tension in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: The uplift resistance in cohesive soils must account for the adhesion along the pile-soil interface. The adhesion values are the same as those used for compression but the resistance factor is lower.

subsections.title: Resistance Changes After Driving
subsections.body: This section covers time-dependent changes in pile resistance after driving, including relaxation (resistance decrease) and soil setup (resistance increase). These phenomena significantly affect the relationship between driving resistance and long-term static capacity.
key_points: Relaxation: resistance decreases over time after driving (primarily toe resistance in dense fine-grained soils)
Setup: resistance increases over time as excess pore pressures dissipate (primarily shaft resistance in clays)
Setup factor = R_n(t)/R_n(EOD); ranges from 1.2 in sands to 5.5+ in sensitive clays
Setup primarily affects shaft resistance in clays; may take days to years
Relaxation most common in dense silts, shales, and weathered rock
AASHTO requires restrike testing when setup or relaxation is expected
Pore pressure estimation during driving from Eq 7-47 and Figure 7-35
equations: Eq 7-42: R_setup = R_n(t) / R_n(EOD) (setup factor definition)
Eq 7-43: R_n(t) = R_n(EOD) * [1 + A * log10(t/t_EOD)] (Skov and Denver 1988 setup equation)
Eq 7-44: A = setup rate parameter (0.2 for sand, 0.6 for clay, Table 7-16)
Eq 7-45: R_setup = (Q_t - Q_EOD) / Q_EOD (measured setup from restrike)
Eq 7-46: R_n_design = R_n(EOD) + phi_setup * R_setup (design resistance including setup)
Eq 7-47: Delta_u / sigma'_v0 = (sigma'_v0 + Delta_sigma_v) * A_f - sigma'_v0 (pore pressure from driving)

subsections.title: Relaxation
subsections.body: Relaxation is a decrease in pile resistance over time after driving. It is most commonly observed in dense silts, shales, and weathered rock where driving generates negative pore pressures that temporarily increase effective stresses. As the negative pore pressures dissipate, resistance decreases.

subsections.title: Soil Setup
subsections.body: Soil setup is the increase in pile resistance over time, primarily due to dissipation of excess positive pore water pressures generated during driving in cohesive soils. The rate and magnitude depend on soil type, sensitivity, permeability, and pile type.

subsections.title: Design Considerations for Setup and Relaxation
subsections.body: Designers must determine whether to rely on setup or account for relaxation. Setup can be incorporated using the Skov-Denver equation with appropriate resistance factors. Restrike testing is required to verify assumed setup values.

subsections.title: Nominal Lateral Resistance
subsections.body: The nominal lateral resistance of driven piles is typically evaluated using p-y analysis methods as detailed in Section 7.3.7. For the strength limit state, the structural capacity of the pile under combined axial and lateral loading must be checked.
key_points: Lateral resistance evaluation uses p-y methods (detailed in Section 7.3.7)
Strength limit state requires structural check under combined loading
Refer to Chapter 8 for structural design of piles

subsections.title: Pile Length Estimates for Contract Documents
subsections.body: Discusses procedures for estimating pile lengths for contract documents based on static analysis results. Estimated lengths should be consistent with the required factored resistance and the subsurface conditions at each substructure location.
key_points: Estimated pile lengths based on static analysis required for plans and specifications
Order lengths should include contingency for subsurface variability
Pile length estimates should consider setup/relaxation effects

subsections.title: Groundwater Effects and Buoyancy
subsections.body: Groundwater affects pile capacity through effective stress changes and buoyancy effects on the pile. Effective stress reduction below the water table reduces both shaft and toe resistance. The buoyant unit weight of the pile below the water table reduces its effective weight. Artesian conditions require special consideration.
key_points: Effective stress below water table reduces shaft and toe resistance
Buoyant pile weight affects net downward load on pile
Artesian conditions can significantly reduce effective stresses and capacity
Perched water tables and seasonal fluctuations must be considered
Use lowest anticipated groundwater table for conservative design

subsections.title: Artesian Conditions
subsections.body: Artesian pressure conditions reduce effective stresses below the artesian pressure head elevation, significantly reducing shaft and toe resistance. Static analysis must use the reduced effective stresses.

subsections.title: Scour
subsections.body: Scour at bridge foundations removes soil around piles, reducing shaft resistance and lateral support. Design must account for both long-term aggradation/degradation and contraction/local scour. AASHTO requires piles be designed for the full depth of scour at the design flood (100-year) for strength limit and check flood (500-year) for extreme event.
key_points: Three scour components: long-term degradation, contraction scour, local scour
Strength limit: full scour depth at design flood (100-year)
Extreme event: full scour at check flood (500-year), see Section 7.4
Shaft resistance lost in scour zone must be subtracted from total resistance
Lateral support lost in scour zone increases pile unsupported length
Must evaluate stream migration potential
Refer to HEC-18 (Arneson et al. 2012) for scour depth calculation
figures: Figure 7-36: Scour effects on pile resistance and lateral support
tables: Table 7-17: Design scour depths by flood event (AASHTO requirements)

subsections.title: Downdrag
subsections.body: Downdrag occurs when soil around a pile settles more than the pile, applying downward drag force (negative shaft resistance). The drag force acts as an additional load on the pile and must be considered in the strength limit state. Common causes include consolidation of soft clays under fill, lowering of the groundwater table, and settlement of liquefied soils after an earthquake. The neutral plane is the depth where the pile and soil settlement are equal.
key_points: Downdrag = negative shaft resistance from soil settling more than the pile
Treated as additional factored load, NOT reduced resistance per AASHTO
Drag load computed using alpha method (cohesive) or beta method (cohesionless)
Neutral plane: depth where pile and soil settlement are equal
Common causes: fill on soft clay, GWT lowering, adjacent surcharge, liquefaction
Bitumen coatings can reduce downdrag but reduce positive shaft resistance too
See Section 7.3.6 for service limit state downdrag (settlement-based approach)
figures: Figure 7-27: Downdrag mechanism on driven pile
Figure 7-28: Neutral plane concept for downdrag

sections.title: Service Limit States
sections.body: This section addresses the service limit state design of driven pile foundations, focusing on deformation control. It covers tolerable deformations, load-settlement behavior (S-0 concept), construction point concept, pile group settlement estimation, downdrag-induced settlement, and lateral deflection analysis. Settlement methods include Meyerhof SPT/CPT methods for cohesionless soils, equivalent footing methods for cohesive soils, Janbu tangent modulus method, and the neutral plane method for downdrag.
key_points: Service limit state controls deformations to tolerable levels
Angular distortion limit typically 0.004-0.008 for bridges (Table 7-18)
S-0 concept: structural load-settlement behavior including elastic compression
Construction point concept accounts for settlement occurring before loads applied
Pile group settlement typically 1.5-3x single pile settlement
Meyerhof SPT/CPT methods for cohesionless group settlement
Equivalent footing method for cohesive soil group settlement
Janbu tangent modulus method as alternative settlement approach
Neutral plane method for downdrag settlement analysis
p-y method for lateral deflection with group effects (p-multipliers)

sections.applicability: Deformation-controlled design ensuring pile foundation movements are within tolerable limits for the supported structure.

subsections.title: Tolerable Deformations
subsections.body: Establishes tolerable deformation criteria for pile-supported structures. Angular distortion (differential settlement / span length) is the primary criterion. For bridges, AASHTO (2014) recommends angular distortion limits. Total settlement limits depend on structure type and function.
key_points: Angular distortion = differential settlement / span length
AASHTO bridge limit: angular distortion < 0.004 for multi-span bridges
Single span bridges more tolerant: angular distortion < 0.008
Total settlement typically 25-50 mm for bridges on piles
Lateral deflection limits depend on structural requirements and utility connections
Table 7-18 provides tolerable movement criteria for various structure types
figures: Figure 7-37: Angular distortion definition and tolerable limits
tables: Table 7-18: Tolerable movement criteria for highway bridges and structures

subsections.title: S-0 Concept (Load-Settlement Behavior)
subsections.body: The S-0 (load-settlement) concept describes the relationship between applied load and pile head settlement. Settlement includes elastic compression of the pile, movement of the pile toe into the soil, and elastic compression of the soil beneath the pile toe. The shape of the S-0 curve depends on whether the pile is friction or end-bearing dominated.
key_points: S-0 curve: complete load vs settlement relationship for a pile
Three settlement components: pile elastic compression, toe movement, soil compression below toe
Friction piles: gradual curving S-0 with large elastic compression
End-bearing piles: stiff response until toe capacity mobilized, then rapid settlement
Davisson offset method defines failure load from S-0 curve
Typical failure settlement = pile elastic compression + 4.0 mm + D/120
figures: Figure 7-38: Typical S-0 curves for friction and end-bearing piles
Figure 7-39: Davisson failure criterion applied to S-0 curve

subsections.title: Construction Point Concept
subsections.body: The construction point concept recognizes that some settlement occurs during construction before the superstructure is connected. Settlement occurring before the connection is made does not affect the structure. Design should evaluate settlement under incremental loading at each construction stage.
key_points: Settlement before superstructure connection does not affect angular distortion
Construction sequence timing affects how much settlement impacts the structure
Incremental loading analysis recommended for each construction stage
Figure 7-40: Construction point concept illustration
Particularly important for approach fills on soft ground
figures: Figure 7-40: Construction point concept for settlement evaluation
Figure 7-41: Example construction sequence with settlement stages

subsections.title: Recommended Procedure for Settlement Analysis
subsections.body: Recommends a systematic procedure for evaluating pile group settlement, considering the construction sequence, load increments, and appropriate analysis methods based on soil type.
key_points: Step 1: Determine construction sequence and load increments
Step 2: Estimate elastic compression of pile
Step 3: Estimate group settlement below pile toe using appropriate method
Step 4: Sum components and compare to tolerable limits
Select analysis method based on soil type and available data

subsections.title: Pile Group Settlement
subsections.body: Presents methods for estimating settlement of pile groups, which is generally larger than single pile settlement due to the increased zone of influence. The equivalent footing approach models the group as a shallow footing at some depth below the pile toe level. Different methods are used for cohesionless and cohesive soils.
key_points: Group settlement typically 1.5-3x single pile settlement for friction piles
End-bearing groups on rock or dense sand may have settlement = single pile settlement
Equivalent footing concept: group modeled as footing at 2/3 pile embedment depth
Cohesionless soils: Meyerhof SPT and CPT methods (semi-empirical)
Cohesive soils: equivalent footing with consolidation analysis
Janbu tangent modulus method as general alternative
Neutral plane method for downdrag settlement

subsections.title: Elastic Compression of Pile
subsections.body: Elastic compression of the pile itself is a significant component of total pile head settlement, particularly for long piles. It depends on the load distribution along the pile, the pile cross-section, and the elastic modulus of the pile material.
key_points: Elastic compression = P*L / (A*E) for uniform load (end-bearing)
For friction piles: 0.5 * P*L / (A*E) since load decreases linearly with depth
Composite piles: sum elastic compression of each material segment
Can be 10-30 mm or more for long piles
equations: Eq 7-48: delta_e = P*L / (A*E) (elastic compression, end bearing)
Eq 7-49: delta_e = 0.5 * P*L / (A*E) (elastic compression, uniform shaft resistance)
figures: Figure 7-42: Load distribution assumptions for elastic compression calculation

subsections.title: Settlement of Pile Groups in Cohesionless Soils
subsections.body: For pile groups in cohesionless soils, the Meyerhof (1976) SPT and CPT methods provide semi-empirical estimates of group settlement. These methods correlate group settlement to the group load, group dimensions, and in-situ test data. The SPT method uses corrected N60 values and the CPT method uses average cone tip resistance in the influence zone below the pile toe.
key_points: Meyerhof SPT method: s = (q_net * B_g * I) / (N60_bar) (Eq 7-50)
Meyerhof CPT method: s = (q_net * B_g * I) / (2 * q_c_bar) (Eq 7-52)
Influence factor I = 1 - D / (8 * B_g) >= 0.5
Average N60 or q_c from pile toe to B_g below pile toe
Settlement increases with group width and applied stress
Typically provides reasonable estimates for normally consolidated sands
equations: Eq 7-50: s = q * sqrt(B_g) / (0.96 * N60_bar) (Meyerhof SPT settlement, mm)
Eq 7-51: I = 1 - D / (8 * B_g) >= 0.5 (depth influence factor)
Eq 7-52: s = q * sqrt(B_g) / (2 * q_c_bar) (Meyerhof CPT settlement, mm)
Eq 7-53: B_g = (n-1)*s + b (group width, where s = pile spacing, b = pile diameter)
Eq 7-54: q = Q_g / (B_g * Z_g) (average applied stress on equivalent footing)
figures: Figure 7-43: Equivalent footing concept for pile group in cohesionless soil

subsections.title: Settlement of Pile Groups in Cohesive Soils
subsections.body: For pile groups in cohesive soils, the equivalent footing method places the footing at 2/3 of the pile embedment depth. The load spreads at 2V:1H below the equivalent footing. Consolidation settlement is computed for each sublayer using the compression index Cc or recompression index Cr. The method accounts for preconsolidation pressure to distinguish between normally consolidated and overconsolidated conditions.
key_points: Equivalent footing at 2/3 pile embedment depth (D_b = 2D/3)
Load spreads at 2V:1H below equivalent footing
Settlement computed layer by layer using Cc/(1+e0) * log10(sigma'_f/sigma'_0)
NC soils: use Cc; OC soils: use Cr up to preconsolidation pressure, then Cc
Stress distribution computed at midpoint of each sublayer
Total settlement = sum of sublayer settlements
Must check influence depth (10% of overburden stress increase)
equations: Eq 7-55: s = SUM[Cc_i/(1+e0_i) * H_i * log10(sigma'_f_i / sigma'_0_i)] (NC settlement)
Eq 7-56: s = SUM[Cr_i/(1+e0_i) * H_i * log10(sigma'_f_i / sigma'_0_i)] (OC settlement, sigma'_f < sigma'_p)
Eq 7-57: s = SUM[Cr_i/(1+e0_i)*H_i*log10(sigma'_p_i/sigma'_0_i) + Cc_i/(1+e0_i)*H_i*log10(sigma'_f_i/sigma'_p_i)] (OC becoming NC)
Eq 7-58: Delta_sigma_v = Q_g / ((B_g + z_i)*(Z_g + z_i)) (stress increase at depth z_i below equivalent footing)
figures: Figure 7-44: Equivalent footing for pile group in cohesive soil
Figure 7-45: 2V:1H load spread below equivalent footing
Figure 7-46: Compression curve showing Cc and Cr on e-log(sigma') plot
Figure 7-47: Settlement computation for layered cohesive profile
tables: Table 7-19: Typical compression index Cc and recompression index Cr values by soil type

subsections.title: Time Rate of Settlement
subsections.body: For cohesive soils, consolidation settlement occurs over time as excess pore water pressures dissipate. The time rate is governed by the coefficient of consolidation cv, the drainage path length, and the drainage conditions (single or double drainage).
key_points: Degree of consolidation U(t) from Terzaghi 1-D consolidation theory
Time factor Tv = cv * t / H_dr^2
Double drainage: H_dr = H/2; single drainage: H_dr = H
90% consolidation typically used for design
Horizontal drainage (radial consolidation) can accelerate settlement
cv from laboratory consolidation tests (odometer) or back-calculated from field data
equations: Eq 7-59: T_v = c_v * t / H_dr^2 (time factor for consolidation)

subsections.title: Settlement in Layered Soils
subsections.body: For layered soil profiles, settlement is computed separately for each layer and summed. The stress distribution must account for load spreading through different soil types.

subsections.title: Janbu Tangent Modulus Method
subsections.body: The Janbu (1963, 1967) tangent modulus method provides an alternative approach for settlement estimation using the tangent constrained modulus M = 1/mv as a function of stress level. The method is applicable to all soil types and uses a modulus number m and stress exponent j to characterize the soil compressibility.
key_points: Alternative to Cc/Cr approach; applicable to all soil types
Tangent constrained modulus M = 1/m_v varies with stress level
Three soil types: j=0 (normally consolidated clay), j=0.5 (silt/sand), j=1 (dense sand/till)
Modulus number m from Table 7-20 based on soil type and density
Method accounts for stress-dependent compressibility
Particularly useful for mixed or non-standard soil profiles
equations: Eq 7-60: epsilon = integral of d_sigma / M(sigma) (strain from stress increase)
Eq 7-61: M = m * sigma_r * (sigma'_v / sigma_r)^(1-j) for j > 0 (tangent modulus)
Eq 7-62: M = m * sigma_r / (1 + e_0) for j = 0 (NC clay tangent modulus)
Eq 7-63: epsilon = (1/m) * ln(sigma'_f / sigma'_0) for j = 0 (NC clay strain)
Eq 7-64: epsilon = (2/m) * [sqrt(sigma'_f/sigma_r) - sqrt(sigma'_0/sigma_r)] for j = 0.5 (silt strain)
Eq 7-65: epsilon = (1/m) * (sigma'_f - sigma'_0) / sigma_r for j = 1 (dense sand strain)
Eq 7-66: s = SUM(epsilon_i * H_i) (total settlement from strain and layer thickness)
Eq 7-67: OC strain uses reloading modulus number m_r
Eq 7-68: For OC soil becoming NC: strain = OC part + NC part
Eq 7-69: sigma_r = 100 kPa (reference stress)
figures: Figure 7-48: Janbu tangent modulus concept (M vs sigma') for different soil types
tables: Table 7-20: Janbu modulus number m and stress exponent j by soil type

subsections.title: Neutral Plane Method for Settlement
subsections.body: The neutral plane method (Fellenius 1989, 2004) provides a rational approach for evaluating pile settlement considering the load transfer mechanism along the pile. The neutral plane is the depth where the relative pile-soil movement is zero. Above the neutral plane, the soil settles more than the pile (negative shaft resistance/downdrag). Below the neutral plane, the pile settles more than the soil (positive shaft resistance). Settlement is computed at the neutral plane depth.
key_points: Neutral plane: depth where pile and soil settlement are equal
Above neutral plane: soil settles more than pile (negative shaft resistance)
Below neutral plane: pile settles more than soil (positive shaft resistance)
Settlement at neutral plane = pile elastic compression + toe movement
Method integrates strength and service limit states into single framework
Figure 7-49 illustrates the unified neutral plane diagram
figures: Figure 7-49: Neutral plane method for downdrag settlement evaluation

subsections.title: Downdrag Settlement
subsections.body: Addresses the service limit state evaluation of downdrag, where the pile settlement due to downdrag forces must be within tolerable limits. The neutral plane approach is used to compute settlement rather than treating downdrag as additional load (which is the strength limit state approach).
key_points: Service limit state: downdrag evaluated as settlement, not additional load
Neutral plane method (Fellenius 1989, Siegel 2013) for settlement computation
Settlement = pile compression above neutral plane + toe settlement
Bitumen coatings reduce downdrag forces but also reduce positive shaft resistance
Must check both strength (drag load) and service (settlement) limit states
equations: Eq 7-70: s_downdrag = delta_pile + delta_toe (total downdrag settlement)
Eq 7-71: delta_pile = integral(P(z)/(A*E)) dz from 0 to neutral plane (pile elastic compression)
Eq 7-72: delta_toe = f(Q_toe, soil stiffness) (toe settlement from load transfer)
figures: Figure 7-50: Neutral plane method for downdrag settlement

subsections.title: Neutral Plane Approach for Downdrag
subsections.body: The neutral plane is found by constructing the load distribution along the pile from both the top (dead load + drag force) and bottom (toe + positive shaft resistance). The intersection defines the neutral plane depth.

subsections.title: Settlement Computation
subsections.body: Once the neutral plane is located, the pile settlement is computed as the sum of elastic pile compression from the pile head to the neutral plane and the toe settlement. The toe settlement can be estimated from load-transfer curves or published correlations.

subsections.title: Lateral Deflection Analysis
subsections.body: Covers methods for evaluating lateral deflection of single piles and pile groups under lateral loads. The p-y method is the primary approach, modeling the soil-pile interaction using nonlinear springs (p-y curves) along the pile length. Group effects are accounted for using p-multipliers that reduce the p-y spring stiffness for piles within a group. The strain wedge method is also discussed as an alternative approach.
key_points: p-y method is the primary lateral analysis approach
p-y curves model nonlinear soil-pile interaction springs
Different p-y curves for different soil types (soft clay, stiff clay, sand)
Fixed vs free head conditions significantly affect deflection and moment
Group effects via p-multipliers (0.2-1.0 depending on position and spacing)
Leading row piles have higher p-multipliers than trailing rows
Strain wedge method suitable for short stiff piles
Computer programs: LPILE, COM624P, GROUP, FB-MultiPier
equations: Eq 7-73: EI * d4y/dx4 + P_x * d2y/dx2 - p = 0 (beam on nonlinear foundation differential equation)
figures: Figure 7-51: p-y curve concept and typical shapes for different soil types
Figure 7-52: Single pile p-y model (beam on nonlinear springs)
Figure 7-53: Fixed vs free head pile deflection and moment distributions
tables: Table 7-21: Recommended p-y curve types by soil condition
Table 7-22: Input parameters for p-y curves by soil type

subsections.title: Pile Head Fixity
subsections.body: The degree of rotational restraint at the pile head (fixed, free, or partial fixity) significantly affects the lateral deflection and bending moment distribution. Fixed head conditions reduce deflection but increase the negative moment at the pile head. Free head conditions allow rotation and result in larger deflection but lower pile head moments.

subsections.title: Lateral Design Methods Overview
subsections.body: Two primary methods for lateral pile analysis: the p-y method (most common for long flexible piles) and the strain wedge method (better for short stiff piles). The p-y method models the pile as a beam on nonlinear springs. The strain wedge method computes passive soil resistance using a 3D failure wedge.

subsections.title: p-y Method
subsections.body: The p-y method solves the beam-on-nonlinear-foundation differential equation (Eq 7-73) using iterative finite difference techniques. Different p-y curve formulations are used for different soil types: Matlock (1970) for soft clay, Reese et al. (1975) for stiff clay below water table, Welch and Reese (1972) for stiff clay above water table, Reese et al. (1974) for sand, and API (1993) for sand. Software programs LPILE and COM624P automate this analysis.
key_points: Beam on nonlinear foundation: EI*d4y/dx4 + Px*d2y/dx2 - p = 0
Matlock (1970): soft clay below water table
Reese et al. (1975): stiff clay below water table
Welch and Reese (1972): stiff clay above water table
Reese et al. (1974): sand
API (1993): sand (alternative to Reese et al.)
Evans and Duncan (1982): weak rock
Iterative solution by finite difference method
Results: deflection, moment, shear, and soil reaction profiles

subsections.title: Strain Wedge Method
subsections.body: The strain wedge method (Norris 1986, Ashour et al. 1998) models the soil failure around a laterally loaded pile using a three-dimensional passive wedge. It relates the horizontal soil resistance to the horizontal strain in the passive wedge and provides p-y curves as output. The method is particularly suitable for short stiff piles and layered soils.

subsections.title: Single Pile Lateral Analysis
subsections.body: For single piles, the p-y analysis determines the lateral deflection, rotation, bending moment, shear force, and soil reaction distribution along the pile length. The analysis is performed for each load combination (service, strength, extreme event). Critical output includes maximum deflection (usually at pile head) and maximum bending moment (usually 3-8 pile diameters below ground).

subsections.title: Pile Group Lateral Analysis
subsections.body: For pile groups under lateral loading, the p-y curves are modified using p-multipliers to account for pile-soil-pile interaction (shadowing) effects. Leading row piles have higher p-multipliers than trailing rows because they push into undisturbed soil. P-multipliers depend on pile spacing, number of rows, and row position. Brown et al. (1988) and others have developed p-multiplier values from full-scale lateral load tests.
key_points: P-multipliers reduce p-y curves for group effects (shadowing)
Leading row: fm = 0.70-1.0; second row: fm = 0.40-0.85; third+ rows: fm = 0.30-0.70
P-multipliers depend on spacing (3D to 5D typical range)
Table 7-23: p-multiplier values from AASHTO (2014)
Table 7-24: p-multiplier values from research by Brown, Rollins, and others
Table 7-25: Summary of full-scale group lateral load tests
Programs GROUP and FB-MultiPier handle group lateral analysis
Rigid cap assumption used for most group analyses

Figure 7-55: Row position effect on p-multipliers
Figure 7-56: Shadowing effect in pile groups under lateral load

subsections.title: Lateral Squeeze
subsections.body: Lateral squeeze occurs when soft soils are loaded by an embankment adjacent to a pile-supported abutment, causing lateral soil movements that load the piles horizontally. This is evaluated using Eq 7-74 and 7-75 to estimate the lateral force on piles from the embankment-induced soil movement.
key_points: Soft soil under embankment can squeeze laterally toward bridge piles
Lateral soil movement imposes horizontal forces on piles
Most critical for abutment piles adjacent to approach embankments
Checked when soft layer thickness < 3x embankment height
Factor of safety against lateral squeeze from Eq 7-74
If FOS < 1.5, lateral pile analysis including imposed soil movement required
equations: Eq 7-74: FOS = (2 * c_u * (1 + D_s/(B_e * sqrt(2)))) / (gamma_fill * H_fill) (FOS against lateral squeeze)
Eq 7-75: y_s = f(p, x, soil properties) (lateral soil movement profile for pile loading)

Figure 7-58: Lateral squeeze evaluation geometry

subsections.title: Overall Stability
subsections.body: Overall stability of the pile-supported structure must be checked, particularly for bridge abutments on slopes, retaining structures, and piles near embankment edges. The global stability analysis includes the pile foundation and surrounding soil mass using limit equilibrium slope stability methods.
key_points: Global stability check required per AASHTO for slopes and abutments
Limit equilibrium methods (Bishop, Spencer) used for global stability
Resistance factor phi_os = 0.65 for overall stability
Piles contribute to stability through shear and moment resistance
Must check stability during all construction stages
figures: Figure 7-59: Overall stability analysis for pile-supported abutment

sections.title: Extreme Event Limit States
sections.body: This section addresses pile foundation design for extreme events including scour during the check flood, seismic loading, ice loads, and vessel collision. These are low probability, high consequence events with higher resistance factors than strength limit states. The section includes detailed seismic design procedures with site classification, spectral acceleration computation, and liquefaction assessment.
key_points: Extreme events: check flood scour, seismic, ice, vessel collision
Higher resistance factors than strength limit states (phi = 1.0 for many cases)
Seismic design: site class, spectral acceleration, liquefaction assessment
Check flood (500-year) scour depth used for extreme event
Combined extreme events evaluated per AASHTO load combinations

sections.applicability: Design for low-probability, high-consequence loading events per AASHTO extreme event limit state requirements.

subsections.title: Scour During Check Flood
subsections.body: For the extreme event limit state, the full scour depth at the check flood (500-year event) is used. All shaft resistance and lateral support in the scour zone is removed. The pile must still have adequate factored resistance below the scour depth.
key_points: Check flood = 500-year event per AASHTO
Full scour depth at check flood for extreme event design
Remove all resistance in scour zone
Pile must develop adequate resistance below scour depth
Lateral support loss increases effective unsupported pile length

subsections.title: Seismic Design
subsections.body: Comprehensive seismic design procedures for pile foundations including site classification, seismic hazard analysis, spectral acceleration computation, and liquefaction potential assessment. Site classification per AASHTO uses shear wave velocity in the upper 30 m (Vs30), SPT N-value (N-bar), or undrained shear strength (su-bar). Site factors Fpga, Fa, and Fv modify the mapped spectral accelerations for local site conditions. Seismic zones determine the level of analysis required.
key_points: Site classification: Class A (hard rock) through F (special study) per Table 7-26
Three site classification criteria: Vs30, average N60 in upper 30 m, average su in upper 30 m
Site factors Fpga, Fa (short period), Fv (long period) from Tables 7-27 through 7-29
Seismic zones 1-4 based on SD1 value (Table 7-30)
Zone 1: SD1 < 0.15 (low seismic); Zone 4: SD1 >= 0.50 (high seismic)
Spectral acceleration Csm from Eq 7-76 through 7-79
Liquefaction assessment required for Zones 3 and 4
Liquefaction triggers for saturated loose sand: N1_60 < 25 and PGA >= 0.10g
equations: Eq 7-76: As = Fpga * PGA (design peak ground acceleration)
Eq 7-77: SDS = Fa * Ss (design short-period spectral acceleration)
Eq 7-78: SD1 = Fv * S1 (design 1-second spectral acceleration)
Eq 7-79: Csm = SDS for Tm <= Ts; Csm = SD1/Tm for Tm > Ts (seismic response coefficient)
Eq 7-80: Ts = SD1/SDS (corner period between constant accel and constant velocity)

subsections.title: Ice Loads and Vessel Collision
subsections.body: Covers extreme event loading from ice forces and vessel collision on pile foundations. Ice forces include static thermal expansion, dynamic ice breaking, and static ice pressure. Vessel collision forces depend on vessel type, size, speed, and waterway geometry.
key_points: Ice loads: static thermal, dynamic breaking, pressure (Eq 7-81 through 7-83)
Dynamic ice force: F = Cn * p * t * w (Eq 7-82)
Static ice pressure: F = Ca * p * t * w (Eq 7-83)
Vessel collision: F = 0.5 * m * v^2 / a (kinetic energy approach, Eq 7-84)
AASHTO LRFD Guide Specifications for Vessel Collision (AASHTO 2010)
Pier protection structures (fender systems, dolphins) can reduce collision loads
equations: Eq 7-81: F_ice_thermal = alpha * E_ice * t * w * Delta_T (thermal ice force)
Eq 7-82: F_ice_dynamic = C_n * p * t * w (dynamic ice breaking force)
Eq 7-83: F_ice_static = C_a * p * t * w (static ice pressure force)

subsections.title: Combined Extreme Events
subsections.body: AASHTO load combinations for extreme events require evaluation of different combinations of extreme loads with permanent and transient loads. Load factors and resistance factors specific to extreme event limit states apply.
key_points: Extreme Event I: earthquake + permanent loads + live load fraction
Extreme Event II: ice/collision/check flood + permanent loads + live load
Resistance factor phi = 1.0 for geotechnical resistance in extreme events
Multiple extreme events not combined simultaneously (e.g., no earthquake + vessel collision)

sections.title: Minimum Pile Penetration Requirements
sections.body: Discusses minimum pile penetration depth requirements to ensure adequate resistance, group behavior, and protection against scour and other adverse conditions. Minimum penetration may be controlled by lateral resistance requirements, scour protection, downdrag, or liquefaction zone penetration rather than axial capacity alone.
key_points: Minimum penetration governed by lateral resistance, not just axial capacity
Must penetrate below scour depth to develop adequate resistance
Liquefaction zones: piles must penetrate through liquefiable layers into competent material
Soft/organic soils: penetrate through soft layers to bearing stratum
Frost heave: penetrate below frost depth in heave-susceptible soils
Minimum 10 feet into competent bearing stratum recommended
Seismic zones 3-4: penetrate through potentially liquefiable layers plus 3 pile diameters
figures: Figure 7-66: Minimum penetration requirements for various conditions

sections.title: Determination of Rndr (Nominal Driving Resistance)
sections.body: Presents the methodology for determining the nominal driving resistance Rndr required to ensure adequate long-term static resistance. Rndr accounts for the difference between resistance at the time of driving (end of drive or restrike) and the long-term static resistance including setup and relaxation effects. The relationship between Rndr and the required nominal resistance depends on whether setup or relaxation is expected.
key_points: Rndr = nominal resistance to be verified during driving
Rndr accounts for setup (increases Rn over time) and relaxation (decreases Rn over time)
If no setup/relaxation: Rndr = Rn (driving resistance equals required nominal resistance)
With setup: Rndr < Rn (can accept lower driving resistance, long-term setup will increase capacity)
With relaxation: Rndr > Rn (need higher driving resistance, resistance will decrease over time)
AASHTO Table 10.5.5.2.3-1 provides resistance factors for driving with setup
Eq 7-85 and 7-86 relate Rndr to factored resistance requirements
Table 7-32 provides phi factors for Rndr determination by verification method
equations: Eq 7-85: R_r = phi * R_ndr + phi_setup * R_setup (factored resistance with setup)
Eq 7-86: R_ndr = (R_r - phi_setup * R_setup) / phi (required nominal driving resistance)

Figure 7-68: Relationship between Rndr, Rn, and setup

sections.title: Drivability Analysis
sections.body: This section covers the evaluation of pile drivability, which is one of the most important yet frequently overlooked aspects of driven pile design. A pile must have a drivability limit in excess of the soil resistance to be overcome during driving. The section discusses factors affecting drivability, methods for determining drivability, and the relationship between drivability and pile type. Three methods are presented: wave equation analysis, dynamic testing and analysis, and static load tests.
key_points: Drivability evaluation is one of the most common deficiencies in driven pile design practice
Pile impedance EA/C is the primary controlling factor for drivability
Two drivability requirements: sufficient stiffness to transmit driving forces AND sufficient strength to withstand driving stresses
Three drivability evaluation methods: wave equation analysis, dynamic testing, static load tests
Wave equation is the most practical design-stage tool for drivability assessment
Must account for soil setup and relaxation effects during driving
For steel H-piles: increase flange width to improve impedance without increasing soil resistance
For pipe piles: increase wall thickness to improve impedance
Concrete piles: increasing area also increases soil resistance (solid cross section)
Inside-fitting cutting shoe for open-end pipe piles can improve drivability
AASHTO (2014) requires wave equation drivability analysis during design

subsections.title: Factors Affecting Drivability
subsections.body: The primary factors affecting pile drivability include pile impedance (EA/C), pile material strength, and driving equipment characteristics. Pile impedance is the primary controlling factor: once pile material and modulus are selected, only increasing cross-sectional area improves drivability. Pile material strength is a lesser factor since it does not alter impedance, but higher strength allows higher driving stresses. Driving system characteristics (ram weight, stroke, speed) and dynamic soil response (damping, quake) also affect drivability. Installation aids (predrilling, jetting, spudding) can assist in meeting penetration requirements but do not change pile section drivability.
key_points: Pile impedance EA/C is the primary controlling factor
E = elastic modulus, A = cross-sectional area, C = wave speed
Increasing area (for same pile type) is the most effective improvement
Steel H-piles: increase H-pile section size to increase impedance
Pipe piles: increase wall thickness to increase impedance
Pile material strength affects allowable driving stress but not impedance
Driving system: ram weight, stroke, and speed affect energy delivered
Installation aids (predrilling, jetting) assist penetration but do not change drivability
Dynamic soil response (damping, quake) can reduce drivability in some soils

subsections.title: Methods for Determining Pile Drivability
subsections.body: Three methods are available for predicting and/or checking pile drivability, presented in order of increasing cost and reliability: (1) Wave equation analysis, (2) Dynamic testing and analysis, and (3) Static load tests. Wave equation analysis is a computer program that accounts for pile impedance and calculates estimated driving stresses as well as blow count versus nominal resistance. It is the most practical design-stage tool. Dynamic testing provides field measurements during driving to calculate driving stresses and estimate nominal resistance. Static load tests are the most accurate but most expensive method.
key_points: Method 1: Wave equation analysis - design stage tool, most practical
Method 2: Dynamic testing - field verification during pile installation
Method 3: Static load tests - most accurate but requires test program during design
Wave equation: calculates blow count vs resistance and driving stresses
Dynamic testing: provides actual driving stresses and resistance estimates
Static load tests: confirms drivability and resistance by actually driving and loading test pile
Methods 1 and 2 can reduce number of static load tests needed
AASHTO (2014) requires wave equation analysis during design stage

subsections.title: Drivability versus Pile Type
subsections.body: Drivability should be checked during the design stage of all driven piles. It is particularly important for closed end steel pipe piles where the impedance of the steel casing may limit drivability. Thin wall pipe piles may lack the drivability to develop required nominal resistance or achieve necessary penetration depth. Steel H-piles, open pipe piles, prestressed concrete piles, and timber piles are also subject to drivability limitations, particularly as extreme events and the trend to larger nominal resistances require increased penetration depths. The drivability of long prestressed concrete piles can be limited by the pile's tensile strength.
key_points: Drivability check required for all pile types during design stage
Closed end pipe piles: steel casing impedance may limit drivability
Thin wall pipe piles: may lack drivability for required resistance or penetration
Wave equation analysis should be performed to select pile section and wall thickness
Prestressed concrete: drivability may be limited by tensile strength for long piles
Example drivability assessment presented in Section 12.5.3
Section 12.5.8 illustrates wave equation drivability for pipe pile wall thickness selection

sections.title: Considerations for Batter Pile Design and Construction
sections.body: Batter (inclined) piles are driven at an inclination from vertical to resist large static lateral loads or where structural rigidity is required. A battered pile can resist larger horizontal loads and experience less deflection than a vertical counterpart at the same loading level. However, under dynamic or seismic loading, the increased structural stiffness from batter piles generates larger forces. In seismic design, earthquake-induced displacements generate load proportional to stiffness, so batter piles attract more load. Where significant downdrag forces are expected, batter piles should be avoided due to increased bending moments. Figure 7-80 illustrates the variation in foundation response depending on group configuration and batter.
key_points: Batter piles driven at inclination from vertical to resist lateral loads
Effective under static lateral loads; problematic under seismic loading
Seismic design: increased stiffness attracts higher forces to the structure
Avoid batter piles where significant drag forces (downdrag) are expected
Batter angles greater than 1H:3V should be avoided for constructability
Horizontal component of axial load contributes to lateral resistance of the group
If no vertical load applied, batter pile has no horizontal component (behaves as vertical)
Figure 7-80: Foundation response for Cases A (single), B (two vertical), C (batter + vertical)
Group analysis with batter piles follows Section 7.3.7.5 procedures with modifications
Careful assessment of load direction relative to batter orientation is essential

sections.title: Corrosion and Deterioration
sections.body: Corrosion and deterioration of all pile types must be considered for the respective environmental conditions. Section 6.12 of Chapter 6 provides extensive design considerations for aggressive subsurface environments. AASHTO (2014) recommends at minimum an evaluation for steel corrosion particularly in fill soils, low pH soils, and marine environments. For concrete piles, sulfate, chloride, and acid attack should be evaluated. Timber piles are subject to decay from wetting and drying cycles as well as attack from marine borers and insects.
key_points: Steel piles: evaluate corrosion in fill soils, low pH soils, and marine environments
Concrete piles: evaluate sulfate, chloride, and acid attack
Timber piles: evaluate decay from wetting/drying, marine borers, and insects
Refer to Chapter 6 Section 6.12 for detailed corrosion design guidance
AASHTO (2014) Article 10.7.5 addresses pile deterioration requirements

sections.title: Additional Design and Construction Considerations
sections.body: This section covers additional practical design and construction considerations that influence the reliability of static analysis procedures and long-term pile resistance. Topics include minimum pile spacing and cap embedment, large pile size considerations, high rebound soils, soil and pile heave, embankment fill effects, predrilling and jetting effects, soil densification, and plugging of open pile sections. These issues bridge the gap between theoretical design calculations and actual construction performance.
key_points: Minimum pile spacing: 2.5 pile diameters or 30 inches (AASHTO)
Recommended spacing >= 3.0 diameters to avoid construction difficulties
Pile head extends minimum 12 inches into pile cap
Minimum 6 inches concrete cover on all sides of piles in cap
Predrilling/jetting reduces shaft resistance by 50-85% in treated zone
Vibratory installation produces lower resistance than impact driving
Densification can increase friction angle 3-4 degrees in loose to medium sands
Open pipe pile plugging begins at penetration/diameter ratio of 20-35 in dense sands
H-piles more likely to be plugged than pipe piles (smaller flange distance)
Soil heave procedure from Haggerty and Peck (1971) for cohesive soils
Piles through embankments: minimum 10 ft below original grade
Install piles center-out to reduce group densification effects

Eq 7-88: R_n = f_so * A_so + q_p * A_pp (plugged condition resistance for open-end pipe)
Eq 7-89: R_n = f_so * A_so + f_si * A_si + q_p * A_p - W_p (unplugged condition resistance)
Eq 7-90: R_n = 0.8 * C_a * A_s + 4.5 * s_u * A_p (Tomlinson equation for open-end pipe in stiff clay)

subsections.title: Minimum Pile Spacing, Clearance, and Cap Embedment
subsections.body: AASHTO (2014) recommends minimum center-to-center pile spacing of 2.5 pile diameters or 30 inches. Pile cap edge should be greater than 9 inches from the side of the nearest pile. Spacing less than 3.0 diameters can create construction difficulties and reduce group axial and lateral resistances. The pile head should extend a minimum of 12 inches into the pile cap. When a reinforced concrete bent cap is cast in place atop piles, the concrete cover should be a minimum of 6 inches on all sides.
key_points: Minimum spacing: 2.5 pile diameters or 30 inches per AASHTO
Recommended spacing: >= 3.0 diameters to avoid construction difficulties
Cap edge: >= 9 inches from nearest pile side
Pile head: minimum 12 inches into pile cap (6 inches if embedded bars/strands)
Concrete cover: minimum 6 inches on all sides in cast-in-place bent caps

subsections.title: Special Considerations for Large Pile Sizes
subsections.body: AASHTO does not address minimum pile spacing or cap embedment for large diameter open end pipe piles. Brown and Thompson (2015) present limited details. Large diameter pipe pile to cap connections use reinforcing cage and/or shear studs. Minimum spacing approximately 3 pile diameters center-to-center. Pile heads typically extend 3 feet into the pile cap for adequate structural connection.

subsections.title: Identification of High Rebound Soils
subsections.body: During pile driving, the hammer impact causes temporary compression. In certain soil types (dense silty sand, hard silty clay, glacial tills, silt, and other fine grained saturated soils), the deformed soil can spring back close to its original position (high elastic rebound). This is generally due to increased pore water pressure near the pile toe. When pile driving is paused, pore water pressure dissipates and smaller rebound occurs. Pile driving equipment with heavy rams operating at short hammer strokes is helpful in these conditions.
key_points: High rebound in dense silty sand, hard silty clay, glacial tills, saturated fine-grained soils
Caused by increased pore water pressure from driving near pile toe
Leads to refusal-like driving conditions despite incomplete pile penetration
Pausing driving allows pore pressure dissipation and reduced rebound
Heavy rams with short strokes recommended for high rebound soils

subsections.title: Soil and Pile Heave
subsections.body: When piles are driven, soil is displaced causing both upward (heave) and lateral movements of previously driven piles. Greater soil volume displaced = greater heave potential. Heave is particularly troublesome for piles supported primarily by toe resistance, as the pile may be lifted from the bearing stratum. A step-by-step procedure adapted from Haggerty and Peck (1971) for estimating soil and pile heave in saturated insensitive clay is presented. The equilibrium depth d is where upward pushing and downward resisting forces on the pile shaft are equal (Eq 7-87, Figure 7-81).
key_points: Soil displacement from driving causes heave and lateral movements
Detrimental to resistance of previously driven piles and adjacent structures
Toe-bearing piles: heave can lift pile from bearing stratum
Saturated insensitive clays: incompressible behavior, greatest heave potential
Step-by-step heave estimation: volumetric displacement ratio, equilibrium depth d, then heave
Eq 7-87: L% = (D-d)/D for pile length resisting heave
Figure 7-81: Force balance diagram for pile heave estimation
Consider low-displacement piles or predrilling to reduce heave

subsections.title: Piles Driven Through Embankment Fills
subsections.body: Piles driven through approach embankment fills should penetrate a minimum of 10 feet below original grade unless refusal driving conditions are encountered on bedrock or a competent bearing layer. To minimize drag forces, piles should not be driven through embankments constructed over compressible materials until after 90% of primary settlement is complete.
key_points: Minimum penetration: 10 feet below original grade through embankment fill
Delay driving until 90% primary settlement complete to minimize downdrag
Identify potential refusal-causing bearing layers via subsurface exploration
Alternative foundation type may be needed if refusal occurs less than 10 ft below embankment base

subsections.title: Effect of Predrilling, Jetting, and Vibratory Installation on Nominal Resistance
subsections.body: Predrilling, jetting, and vibratory installation methods cause greater soil disturbance than standard impact driving. Shaft resistance in the jetted zone is reduced by approximately 50% per Poulos and Davis (1980). Shaft resistance over a predrilled depth is reduced 50-85% depending on hole size per McClelland et al. (1969). Vibratory installed piles generally develop lower nominal resistance than impact driven piles. Impact driving a specific final depth of vibratory installed piles may restore resistance.
key_points: Jetting reduces shaft resistance by ~50% in jetted zone (Poulos and Davis 1980)
Predrilling reduces shaft resistance by 50-85% depending on hole size
Vibratory installation: lower resistance than impact driving in most cases
Impact driving vibratory-installed piles can restore resistance
Time-dependent soil strength changes (setup) occur equally for both methods
Must evaluate effects on compression, uplift, and lateral resistance

subsections.title: Densification Effects on Nominal Resistance and Installation Conditions
subsections.body: Driving piles in cohesionless soils influences the surrounding soil to a distance of about 3 to 5 pile diameters. Soil displacement and vibrations from driving pile groups can further densify cohesionless materials. Studies indicate friction angle may increase by up to 4 degrees for piles in loose to medium dense sands. Densification can cause significant construction problems if scour, seismic, or other considerations require achieving penetration depths that cannot be achieved. Install piles from center of group outward to reduce group densification effects.
key_points: Densification zone: 3-5 pile diameters from pile in cohesionless soils
Friction angle increase: up to 4 degrees in loose to medium dense sands
Less increase in dense sands or soils with significant fines
Can prevent achieving required penetration depths
Install from center outward to reduce group densification effects
Cofferdam confinement can further aggravate densification
May require low-displacement piles, increased spacing, or installation aids

subsections.title: Plugging of Open Pile Sections
subsections.body: Open pile sections (open-end pipe piles and H-piles) may behave as low displacement piles (coring through soil) or as displacement piles if a soil plug forms near the pile toe. Plugging of pipe piles in medium dense to dense sands generally begins at a penetration-to-diameter ratio of 20 (can be as high as 35). For pipe piles in soft to stiff clays, plugging can occur at ratios of 10 to 20. For large diameter open-end pipe piles (>36 inches), plugging during driving is less likely. The static resistance of an open-end pipe pile should be calculated from the lesser of plugged (Eq 7-88) and unplugged (Eq 7-89) conditions. The Tomlinson equation (Eq 7-90) applies to open-end pipe piles in stiff clays. H-piles are more likely to be plugged than pipe piles due to smaller flange distance. Static load tests are recommended for large diameter open-end pipe piles (>18 inches) due to plugging uncertainty.
key_points: Open pipe piles: core vs plug behavior during driving and under static load
Plugging in dense sand: penetration/diameter ratio of 20-35
Plugging in soft-stiff clay: ratio of 10-20
Large diameter pipe (>36 in): less likely to plug during driving
H-piles: more likely to be plugged (smaller flange gap)
Design resistance = lesser of plugged (Eq 7-88) and unplugged (Eq 7-89) conditions
Interior shaft resistance: typically 1/3 to 1/2 of exterior shaft resistance
Tomlinson (1994): limiting unit toe resistance of 105 ksf for open-end pipes in cohesionless soils
Eq 7-90: Tomlinson equation for open-end pipe in stiff clay with confirmed plug
Forced plugging via constrictor plate (Figures 6-14, 6-15) reduces uncertainty

Figure 7-83: Open toe vs plugged toe mechanisms (Paikowsky and Whitman 1990)
